question: In the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis, which of the following best describes the primary negative feedback mechanism that suppresses TSH secretion?

answers.text: Rising TRH levels from the hypothalamus directly inhibit anterior pituitary thyrotrophs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. TRH from the hypothalamus stimulates TSH release; it does not provide negative feedback. The negative feedback is mediated by thyroid hormones.

answers.text: Elevated circulating free T3 and T4 act on anterior pituitary thyrotrophs to suppress TSH secretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Free T3 and T4 exert negative feedback on the anterior pituitary thyrotrophs (and to a lesser extent on the hypothalamus), reducing TSH secretion. TSH is therefore the most sensitive marker of thyroid status.

answers.text: High TSH levels feed back on the hypothalamus to inhibit TRH release only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. TSH does not directly inhibit hypothalamic TRH in a clinically significant way. The dominant negative feedback is by thyroid hormones (T3/T4) on the pituitary.

answers.text: Reverse T3 (rT3) accumulation suppresses both TRH and TSH secretion simultaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. rT3 is an inactive metabolite; it is not the primary mediator of HPT axis negative feedback. T3 and T4 are the active hormones that suppress TSH.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the HPT axis: TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (pituitary) → T3/T4 (thyroid) → T3/T4 feeds back to suppress TSH. TSH is exquisitely sensitive to small changes in thyroid hormone levels.
Well done. Free T3 and T4 suppress TSH via pituitary negative feedback — this is why TSH is the most sensitive first-line test for thyroid dysfunction.
